summary: Specifies TLS cipher suites that use a pre-shared key to authenticate an ephemeral elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman exchange. They provide perfect forward secrecy, so recorded traffic stays safe even if keys are exposed later. It extends RFC 4279, RFC 4492 and RFC 4785.

plainLanguage.summary: Two friends use a shared secret to prove who they are, then make a fresh one-time code for each chat. Even if someone later learns the shared secret, old chats stay secret.

questions: how to get forward secrecy with tls psk
what are the ecdhe_psk cipher suites
how is the ecdhe_psk premaster secret built
subtitle: TLS cipher suites that use a pre-shared key to authenticate a fresh elliptic curve key exchange, giving forward secrecy.

tldr.problem: Earlier pre-shared key (PSK) cipher suites for TLS either lacked an elliptic curve exchange or did not combine a PSK with ephemeral keys, so there was no PSK suite family that used ECDHE for Perfect Forward Secrecy.
tldr.mechanism: The suites run an Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman exchange with ephemeral keys and authenticate it with a PSK. The premaster secret joins the ECDH result Z with the PSK, and nine cipher suites are registered.
tldr.outcome: The suites provide Perfect Forward Secrecy. Three of the nine use NULL encryption, so they give authentication and integrity only and must not carry sensitive data such as passwords.

today: RFC 5489 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends RFC 4279, RFC 4492 and RFC 4785.

sections.title: What These Suites Add
sections.content:
RFC 4279 defines TLS cipher suites based on pre-shared symmetric keys. RFC 4785 defines authentication-only suites with no encryption, and RFC 4492 defines elliptic curve cipher suites, including Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) key agreement.

RFC 5489 combines these ideas. It specifies suites that use a pre-shared key (PSK) to authenticate an ECDH exchange with ephemeral keys (ECDHE), which provides Perfect Forward Secrecy. Some of the suites provide authentication only. The reader is expected to know RFC 4279, RFC 4492 and RFC 4785 first.

The suites can be negotiated whatever the negotiated TLS version is, and the applicability statement in RFC 4279 applies here as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Some secret-handshake rules already existed. This document mixes them so friends who share a secret can also make a brand-new secret code each time they talk.

sections.title: The ECDHE_PSK Key Exchange
sections.content:
The suites reuse the elliptic curve parameter negotiation of RFC 4492. Instead of the psk case from RFC 4279, the ec_diffie_hellman_psk case MUST be used inside the ServerKeyExchange and ClientKeyExchange messages. These messages carry the EC Diffie-Hellman parameters as RFC 4492 specifies. The PSK identity and identity hint keep the meaning and encoding they have in RFC 4279, and ServerKeyExchange is always sent, even when no identity hint is provided.

The premaster secret is built in two steps. First perform the ECDH computation from RFC 4492, which produces an octet string Z. Then concatenate a uint16 holding the length of Z in octets, Z itself, a uint16 holding the length of the PSK in octets, and the PSK itself. This matches the general premaster structure of RFC 4279, with other_secret holding Z.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side picks a fresh secret number and they combine them into a shared code. Then they stir the old shared secret into the mix, so only friends who know it can end up with the same code.

sections.title: The Cipher Suites
sections.content:
Four suites use SHA-1: TLS_ECDHE_PSK_WITH_RC4_128_SHA (0xC0,0x33), TLS_ECDHE_PSK_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA (0xC0,0x34), TLS_ECDHE_PSK_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA (0xC0,0x35) and TLS_ECDHE_PSK_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA (0xC0,0x36). They match the RFC 4279 suites except that they use an ECDH exchange authenticated with a PSK. The MAC is HMAC with SHA-1. For TLS versions before 1.2 the PRF of that version is used. Otherwise the PRF is the TLS PRF of RFC 5246 with SHA-256.

Two more suites use SHA-2 hashes with AES: TLS_ECDHE_PSK_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA256 (0xC0,0x37) uses HMAC and the TLS PRF with SHA-256, and TLS_ECDHE_PSK_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA384 (0xC0,0x38) uses SHA-384 for both. Before TLS 1.2 the PRF of that version is used.

Finally, three suites use NULL encryption: TLS_ECDHE_PSK_WITH_NULL_SHA (0xC0,0x39), TLS_ECDHE_PSK_WITH_NULL_SHA256 (0xC0,0x3A) and TLS_ECDHE_PSK_WITH_NULL_SHA384 (0xC0,0x3B). They match the corresponding suites above but without encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: The document lists nine ready-made combinations of locks and checkers. Most scramble the messages, and three only check that nobody changed them.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5246, RFC 4785, RFC 4492 and RFC 4279 apply. The NULL-encryption suites provide no confidentiality, so care should be taken not to send sensitive information such as passwords over connections protected by them.

Implementers and administrators should also watch the published statements on recommended cryptographic algorithms, for example about the SHA-1 hash function, when they choose which suites to support.

The nine cipher suite values are assigned from the TLS Cipher Suite registry defined in RFC 5246.
sections.plainLanguage: Three of the suites do not hide messages, so never use them to send secrets like passwords. Also keep an eye on which locks experts say are still strong.
